warmup.q: A payout worker inserts each payout into one Cassandra partition per merchant and deletes the row once the payout is paid. Today 50,000 payouts came and went for M-0042, and 10 are waiting. What does reading the next 10 cost?
options: About 10 rows: deleted rows are gone, so the partition holds 10
About 50,010 entries: every delete left a tombstone the read has to step over
Nothing extra after a few minutes, because compaction removes deleted rows right away
It depends only on the LIMIT, because Cassandra stops after 10 rows
warmup.why: A Cassandra delete writes a tombstone, and compaction may drop it only after gc_grace_seconds, 10 days by default, so other replicas can't bring the row back. A read from the front of the partition steps over every tombstone before it finds 10 live rows. Past 100,000 tombstones in one read, Cassandra aborts the read. The LIMIT counts live rows, not what the node had to read to find them.

sections.h: A table is a map of partitions, and each partition is a sorted list of rows
sections.html:
Lesson 4 packed a whole screen into one DynamoDB item collection: one partition key, many sorted items. Cassandra builds its entire data model on that shape, a partition of sorted rows, and the model is called wide-column. Lesson 2 gave the payment history its own Cassandra table:

CREATE TABLE payments_by_account (
    account_id   text,
    created_at   timestamp,
    payment_id   text,
    merchant_id  text,
    status       text,
    amount_minor bigint,
    currency     text,
    PRIMARY KEY ((account_id), created_at, payment_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (created_at DESC, payment_id ASC);

The inner parentheses hold the partition key; the columns after it are clustering columns. This lesson opens the box: what that key means on one node, what a write leaves on disk, and why deleting rows can make reads slow.

Start from the question the table answers: A-1001's 20 newest payments, out of 50 million. Every row with the same partition key belongs to one partition. The coordinator, whichever node took the request, hashes the partition key to a token, a 64-bit number (A-1001's is -4994511478997274402). The token's place on a ring like lesson 1's picks the nodes that keep copies of the partition, its replicas, usually three. Each replica holds the whole partition, so a query that names the partition key talks only to those nodes. The Partitioning track builds Cassandra's ring properly.

Inside the partition, the rows are kept sorted by the clustering columns: newest created_at first, with payment_id breaking ties. The order is how they sit in memory and on disk, so "the 20 newest" means "the first 20 rows of one partition", and a time window is one contiguous slice: the node seeks to the first row inside the window and reads until it leaves it. Oldest first is the same slice, read from the other end.

That shape gives the family its name, and the name misleads. A partition is Bigtable's row from lesson 1, and the clustering values play the part of its sorted column names, so a partition is a "wide" row that can hold many entries. It has nothing to do with a column store, which keeps each column's values together for reports. Stonebraker and Pavlo describe the wide-column model as a document model with one level of nesting: a partition key, then a sorted list of rows that each have their own columns.

A partition never splits across nodes, so its size is your decision. The Cassandra docs advise under 100,000 rows and under 100 MB. Do the arithmetic before you pick the key: rows in a partition = write rate × how long the partition key stays the same. Keyed by merchant alone, AP3's table grows forever. Add the day, ((merchant_id, day), ...), and a merchant taking 40,000 payments a day fills a partition with 40,000 rows, about 6 MB at 150 bytes a row. The biggest merchant on Black Friday takes 5 a second, 432,000 a day, past the row guideline, so for that table an hour bucket (18,000 rows) is the safer choice. The bucket costs reads: a week of history is 7 day partitions or 168 hour partitions, read in parallel and merged. Size it for your busiest key, not your average one.

The query rules follow from the picture. The partition key needs = on every column, or there's no token and no node to ask. Clustering columns can be restricted only from the left, because that's the only order the rows are in, with at most one range at the end. Anything else means reading rows and throwing most of them away, and CQL refuses unless you add ALLOW FILTERING (section 4). So you build one table per query, and the service writes each payment to every table that needs it.

A partition is a sorted list of rows that Cassandra never edits in place: every write, updates and deletes included, adds a new timestamped piece, and every read merges the pieces it finds. The stepper shows the sorted list. Sections 2 and 3 add the pieces.

try.title: Watch a write land in its sorted place
steps: From the labs folder, start Cassandra 5.0: docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml up -d --wait (about one to two minutes). Load lesson 2's tables: docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml exec cassandra cqlsh -f /sfz/nosql-02-payments.cql.
Open a prompt with docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml exec cassandra cqlsh and run the four statements below. Before the third, predict which rows come back and in which order.
Leave Cassandra running: the next three Try-its use it.

sections.h: Every write is an append: commit log, memtable, SSTable
sections.html:
A payment changes state several times: AUTHORIZED, then CAPTURED, then SETTLED. An Oracle UPDATE finds the block that holds the row and changes it in place, keeping the old value in undo for readers who still need it. The block has to be in memory first, which often means a random read before the write. Cassandra, which Facebook first built for its inbox search, takes the other road: a write never reads anything first, and a file is never changed once it's written.

The write path is lesson 1's LSM tree in one line: the node appends the write to its commit log so it survives a crash, adds it to the memtable, a sorted structure in memory, and acknowledges. When the memtable is full, the node flushes it to disk as an SSTable, an immutable sorted file. Nothing is looked up first. Three things follow, and each one surprises people who come from SQL.

First, INSERT and UPDATE are the same operation, an upsert. An UPDATE of a row that doesn't exist creates it. An INSERT of a primary key that already exists overwrites the columns it names, with no duplicate-key error. "Insert only if absent" needs a lightweight transaction (section 4).

Second, every cell carries its own write timestamp, in microseconds. The Java driver 4.19 stamps each statement with the application server's clock (its default, AtomicTimestampGenerator) unless the statement says USING TIMESTAMP. When a read finds two versions of a cell, the higher timestamp wins, column by column. That rule is called last write wins, and the Replication track's lesson on concurrent writes shows which writes it silently drops. An UPDATE of status writes only the status cell, so after two flushes the row exists as two pieces in two SSTables, and every read stitches them together. The Try-it dumps both pieces.

Third, a read may have to look in the memtable and in several SSTables. Bloom filters, a small summary per file that can answer "this partition is definitely not here", let it skip SSTables, and compaction keeps the count of SSTables down: in the background it merges several into one new file, keeps the newest version of each cell and drops the rest. Which files it merges is the compaction strategy. Size-tiered (STCS) merges files of similar size, and it's still the default in the cassandra.yaml of 5.0.9. Leveled (LCS) arranges files in levels so a read touches fewer of them, at the price of rewriting data more often. Time-window (TWCS) groups data by write time, which suits rows that all expire after the same TTL. Cassandra 5.0 added the Unified Compaction Strategy (UCS), which can be tuned to behave like any of the three; its docs recommend it "for most workloads", and the cassandra_latest.yaml that ships with 5.0 makes it the default. For a new table on 5.0, start with UCS.

sections.h: A delete is a write too: tombstones, TTL and the tombstone storm
sections.html:
Delete a test payment, pay-81655, from A-1001's history. Its three replicas are A, B and C, and C is down for an hour. The first version of a delete removes the row from A and B. Then C comes back, and repair runs. Cassandra compares the replicas' copies, during reads (read repair) and in a background job (anti-entropy repair), and copies over whatever one of them lacks; the Replication track's lesson on leaderless replication builds both. Repair finds that C has a row A and B don't have. Nothing tells repair whether A and B lost the row or deleted it, so it copies the row back. The deleted payment returns.

So Cassandra makes a delete a write. It writes a tombstone, a marker with a timestamp that says "this row was deleted at t". The tombstone takes the same write path to every replica and beats older versions by the same timestamp rule. Repair now has something to spread, and C gets the tombstone too.

How long must a tombstone stay? Until every replica has it. Cassandra can't know when that is, so it keeps each tombstone for gc_grace_seconds, 864,000 seconds (10 days) by default, and only after that lets compaction drop it. That gives operators a deadline: repair every node more often than every 10 days. A node that stays down longer, then rejoins and is repaired, still has the old row, and the tombstone that should shadow it is gone everywhere else. Repair copies the row back, and the delete is undone. Operators call those rows zombies.

A TTL works the same way. INSERT ... USING TTL 86400 gives the cells an expiry 24 hours out, which suits idempotency keys. After that the cells are dead: reads skip them and count them as tombstones, and compaction drops them once gc_grace_seconds have passed.

Now the failure. A payout worker uses a table as a queue: one partition per merchant, one row per payout, sorted by payout id, and the worker deletes each row once the payout is paid. Every delete leaves a tombstone at the front of the partition, and the tombstones stay for 10 days. When the worker asks for the next 10 payouts, the read starts at the front and steps over every tombstone before it finds 10 live rows. After 1,990 paid payouts, it handles 2,000 entries to return 10. With more than 1,000 tombstones in one read Cassandra logs a warning (tombstone_warn_threshold), and with more than 100,000 it aborts the read (tombstone_failure_threshold). That's a tombstone storm, and the Try-it starts one.

There are two fixes. Start the slice after the tombstones: keep the last paid payout id and ask for payout_id > ?, so the node seeks past them, as the figure shows. On the same partition with 1,200 tombstones, that read reports "Read 3 live rows and 0 tombstone cells". Or don't delete at all: put a time bucket in the partition key and let old buckets expire with a TTL, on TWCS, which drops whole expired files. A real work queue belongs in Kafka, where reading a message doesn't delete anything.

try.title: Fill a partition with tombstones
steps: Read TombstoneDemo.kt. It creates payments.payout_queue (partition merchant_id, clustering payout_id), enqueues 2,000 payouts for M-0042, deletes the first 1,990 the way a worker would, and reads the next 10 with tracing on.
Predict how many tombstones that read steps over. Run the demo from the labs folder.
Optional, about a minute: run it again with -Pargs=101000, then look for the reason in the log: docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml logs cassandra | grep -i tombstones | tail -1.

Now a TTL. In cqlsh, run CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS payments.idempotency_keys (idem_key text PRIMARY KEY, payment_id text); and INSERT INTO payments.idempotency_keys (idem_key, payment_id) VALUES ('idem-9b21', 'pay-81724') USING TTL 10; then SELECT idem_key, payment_id, TTL(payment_id) FROM payments.idempotency_keys WHERE idem_key = 'idem-9b21';. Wait 11 seconds, turn TRACING ON and run the SELECT again.

code.title: TombstoneDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.model.l05.demo import com.datastax.oss.driver.api.core.CqlSession import com.datastax.oss.driver.api.core.config.DefaultDriverOption import com.datastax.oss.driver.api.core.config.DriverConfigLoader import com.datastax.oss.driver.api.core.cql.PreparedStatement import com.datastax.oss.driver.api.core.cql.SimpleStatement import com.datastax.oss.driver.api.core.servererrors.ReadFailureException import java.net.InetSocketAddress import java.time.Duration /** * A payout queue in one Cassandra partition: enqueue 2,000 payouts for M-0042, let a worker * delete the ones it has paid, then read the next 10. Run against env/cassandra.yml. * Optional argument: how many payouts the worker has processed (default 1990; try 101000). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val processed = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 1_990 val total = maxOf(2_000, processed + 10) // always leave 10 payouts waiting val config = DriverConfigLoader.programmaticBuilder() .withBoolean(DefaultDriverOption.REQUEST_LOG_WARNINGS, false) // we print the server's warnings ourselves .withDuration(DefaultDriverOption.REQUEST_TIMEOUT, Duration.ofSeconds(10)) .build() CqlSession.builder() .addContactPoint(InetSocketAddress("localhost", 9042)) .withLocalDatacenter("datacenter1") .withConfigLoader(config) .build().use { session -> session.execute("CREATE KEYSPACE IF NOT EXISTS payments WITH replication = {'class': 'SimpleStrategy', 'replication_factor': 1}") session.execute( "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS payments.payout_queue (merchant_id text, payout_id int, amount_minor bigint, " + "PRIMARY KEY ((merchant_id), payout_id))" ) session.execute("TRUNCATE payments.payout_queue") // a queue: the producer appends payouts, the worker deletes each one once it's paid val enqueue = session.prepare("INSERT INTO payments.payout_queue (merchant_id, payout_id, amount_minor) VALUES ('M-0042', ?, 500)") val done = session.prepare("DELETE FROM payments.payout_queue WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' AND payout_id = ?") runAll(session, enqueue, 0 until total) runAll(session, done, 0 until processed) println("enqueued $total payouts, processed and deleted $processed") // the worker asks for the next batch: the 10 oldest payouts still waiting val next = SimpleStatement.newInstance("SELECT payout_id FROM payments.payout_queue WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' LIMIT 10") .setTracing(true) val rs = try { session.execute(next) } catch (e: ReadFailureException) { println("read failed: ${e.message}") return } val ids = rs.all().map { it.getInt("payout_id") } println("next batch: ${ids.size} payouts, ${ids.firstOrNull()} to ${ids.lastOrNull()}") val trace = rs.executionInfo.queryTrace trace.events.map { it.activity ?: "" } .filter { "tombstone" in it } .forEach { println("trace: $it") } println("trace: took ${trace.durationMicros} microseconds on the server") rs.executionInfo.warnings.forEach { println("warning: $it") } } } /** Runs [statement] once per id, at most 256 requests in flight. */ private fun runAll(session: CqlSession, statement: PreparedStatement, ids: IntRange) { ids.chunked(256).forEach { chunk -> chunk.map { session.executeAsync(statement.bind(it)).toCompletableFuture() }.forEach { it.join() } } }

sections.h: Off the key: ALLOW FILTERING, SAI indexes and lightweight transactions
sections.html:
Sooner or later someone needs a query the tables weren't built for. Support wants every FAILED payment from today. The CQL error from lesson 2 offers ALLOW FILTERING, and it's tempting, because on a laptop it works. The Try-it's trace shows what it does: "Submitting range requests on 17 ranges", then "Executing seq scan across 1 sstables", then "Read 7 live rows". The node walked every token range and read every row of every partition to return two. With 50 million payments on 12 nodes, each request reads 50 million rows on 12 nodes. ALLOW FILTERING is fine in one case: when the query also names the partition key, so the cost is one partition, which you've already kept small.

The second option is a new table, failed_payments_by_day, written next to the others. For anything on a hot path that's still the answer.

The third, new in Cassandra 5.0, is a storage-attached index (SAI): CREATE INDEX ... USING 'sai'. Each node indexes only its own data, and the index files are built and compacted along with the memtable and SSTables they describe. A query on status alone now reads only matching rows, but it still asks every node, because any node may hold a FAILED payment: the trace still says 17 ranges. So SAI is right for a query that runs a few times a minute, or to filter inside one partition (account_id = ? AND status = ?). It's wrong for the authorization path, and every write pays to keep it up to date.

The last tool fixes something the write path made impossible. AP4 says an idempotency key may be used once. Two retries of the same payment reach two coordinators at the same moment. Both INSERT the key, both succeed because an insert is an upsert, the later timestamp wins, and both requests believe they created the payment. INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS turns the insert into a lightweight transaction (LWT): the replicas first agree, through a round of the Paxos consensus protocol, that the row is absent, and only then write. The reply has an [applied] column, and when it's False it carries the row that won. The CQL docs warn that LWTs "incur a non-negligible performance cost": a Paxos round adds several round trips between replicas to the write. Use them for the few writes that must not race, like claiming a key. The Transactions track's lesson on transactions in NoSQL shows how Paxos makes this safe, and what Cassandra 6's Accord adds for transactions across partitions.

This lesson treated the cluster as one box that stores partitions. The Partitioning track opens the box, in its lesson on the inside of a Cassandra cluster (the token ring, snitches, gossip, and how a coordinator runs a read or a write) and the one after it, which sets a cluster up from cassandra.yaml and keeps it healthy with nodetool.

refs.title: Apache Cassandra: CQL data manipulation (ALLOW FILTERING, IF NOT EXISTS, USING TTL)
Apache Cassandra 5.0 features: Storage Attached Indexes (project blog)

analogy: Think of a filing drawer for each account, where every payment slip is filed in date order. Nobody ever erases a slip. To change a payment you file a newer slip for it, stamped with the time; to delete one you file a red "void" slip. A reader pulls the slips for a date range and keeps the latest stamp for each payment. Once in a while a clerk recopies the drawer, keeping only the latest slip per payment (compaction), but keeps the void slips for ten days, because two other offices hold copies of the drawer and haven't all seen them yet. A drawer used as an inbox fills with void slips that every reader has to flip past. The analogy breaks on the stamps: a clerk would notice two slips stamped a second apart from two different offices, while Cassandra trusts whichever clock reads later, even a clock that is wrong.
world: In Oracle, a payment's status lives in one row that each UPDATE changes in place. In Cassandra each status change is a new cell with the application server's timestamp, so the clocks on your Quarkus pods matter: keep NTP healthy, or a pod running 2 seconds fast wins arguments it shouldn't. A Kafka consumer that writes payments into Cassandra gets idempotency almost free, because replaying a message writes the same key with the same values. Deletes are where teams get hurt: a table used as a work queue for a settlement batch, or "clean up the processed rows" jobs, fill partitions with tombstones that every read pays for. Put the queue in Kafka, bucket tables by time (sized for your Black Friday merchant, not your average one), and claim idempotency keys with INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS USING TTL 86400, so a Temporal activity that retries finds the key already taken.
mistake: The most common mistake is using a Cassandra table as a queue, or any insert-then-delete pattern on one partition: pending payouts, jobs, outbox rows. It looks harmless, because the table has the right key and deletes return instantly. People expect a delete to remove data, as it does in SQL. Instead every delete adds a tombstone that stays for at least 10 days, and every read that starts at the front of the partition steps over all of them, until reads slow down and then fail at 100,000 tombstones. The fix: keep queues in Kafka; in Cassandra, bucket partitions by time and let old buckets expire with a TTL instead of deleting rows, and read from a saved position (payout_id > ?) so slices start after the dead rows.

compare.title: One status change: Oracle edits a row, Cassandra adds a piece

a.label: Oracle: update in place
a.title: SQL*Plus
a.html: UPDATE payment SET status = 'CAPTURED' WHERE payment_id = 'pay-81723'; -- the block holding the row is read into the buffer cache, changed in place, -- and the old value goes to undo for readers who still need it. -- One row, one current version, one place on disk. COMMIT;

b.label: Cassandra: append and merge
b.title: sstabledump of two SSTables
b.html:
UPDATE payments.payments_by_account SET status = 'CAPTURED' WHERE ...;

== nb-1-big-Data.db  (the original insert, unchanged)
'2026-11-07T09:00:00.000Z', 'pay-81723' | [amount_minor=2500 ts=1794081362991451], ...,
                                          [status=AUTHORIZED ts=1794081362991451]
== nb-2-big-Data.db  (the update: one cell)
'2026-11-07T09:00:00.000Z', 'pay-81723' | [status=CAPTURED ts=1794081383953194]

-- a read merges both pieces; compaction later writes one merged row

compare.note: Oracle keeps one current version of a row in one place, and an update has to find it first. Cassandra never finds anything before a write: it adds the new cell with its timestamp, and the old one stays on disk until compaction merges the files. That's why Cassandra writes are cheap and steady under load, and why reads may touch several files. It's also why there's no "row not found" or "duplicate key" on a plain write, and why a delete has to be a marker rather than an erase.

worked.title: Redesign the payout queue so reads never wade through tombstones

steps.say: Write the access patterns first. The worker asks for the oldest waiting payouts of one merchant; support looks a payout up by id. About 30,000 payouts a day for a busy merchant.
steps.code:
P1  next waiting payouts of a merchant, oldest first   ~every second
P2  one payout by id                                    ~a few per minute
volume: 30,000 payouts a day for M-0042

steps.say: The first draft is a queue: one partition per merchant, delete each row once it's paid. Count what a read meets after one day: tombstones live 10 days, so they pile up.
steps.code:
PRIMARY KEY ((merchant_id), payout_id)       -- delete when paid

after 1 day:   ~30,000 tombstones at the front of M-0042's partition
after 4 days:  ~120,000 -> past tombstone_failure_threshold: P1 fails

steps.say: Stop deleting. Bucket by hour, so a partition only ever holds one hour of payouts, and record the state as a column. Let whole buckets expire after a week with a TTL, on TWCS, which drops expired files whole.
steps.code: CREATE TABLE payouts_by_merchant_hour ( merchant_id text, hour timestamp, payout_id timeuuid, status text, amount_minor bigint, PRIMARY KEY ((merchant_id, hour), payout_id) ) WITH default_time_to_live = 604800 AND compaction = {'class': 'TimeWindowCompactionStrategy', 'compaction_window_unit': 'DAYS', 'compaction_window_size': 1};

steps.say: The worker keeps its position: the hour bucket and the last payout it handled. Each read starts after that point, so it never reads old rows at all. Marking a payout paid is an update of one cell, not a delete.
steps.code: SELECT payout_id, amount_minor FROM payouts_by_merchant_hour WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' AND hour = '2026-11-07 09:00:00+0000' AND payout_id > ? -- the last payout already handled LIMIT 10; UPDATE payouts_by_merchant_hour SET status = 'PAID' WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' AND hour = '2026-11-07 09:00:00+0000' AND payout_id = ?;

steps.say: P2 gets its own small table, written with the payout. It expires with the same TTL, so nothing is ever deleted by hand.
steps.code: CREATE TABLE payout_by_id ( payout_id timeuuid PRIMARY KEY, merchant_id text, hour timestamp, amount_minor bigint ) WITH default_time_to_live = 604800;

lab.title: Build one Cassandra table: sorted partitions, SSTables, tombstones and compaction
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. All twelve fail with NotImplementedError.

Read WideColumnTable.kt. insert, delete, flush and repairFrom are given: writes only ever add a Version to the memtable, and flush turns the memtable into an immutable SSTable. Each Version is a whole row with one timestamp; real Cassandra keeps one per cell.
Write filteringReason, following rules 1 to 5 in its KDoc. The messages are Cassandra's own, from lesson 2's Try-it.

Write mergedPartition: for each clustering key, the newest version across the SSTables and the memtable. Then select: refuse, pick partitions, walk the merged rows, count live rows and tombstones, stop at the limit. Ten tests pass now, including the tombstone storm.

Write compact. The last test is section 3's zombie made real: purge a tombstone after gc_grace, repair from a replica that missed the delete, and the row comes back. Change gcGrace in the test to 60 and watch the first half of that test fail, then put it back.
hints: Rule 1 is one line: if (!q.where.keys.containsAll(key.partitionKey)) return ALLOW_FILTERING.
For rule 3, the restricted columns are q.where.keys + listOfNotNull(q.range?.column). A clustering column at index i >= fixed that's restricted is a gap, unless i == fixed and it's the range.

In mergedPartition, the sources are sstables.mapNotNull { it.partitions[partition] } + listOfNotNull(memtable[partition]). Use newer(version, old) to decide, never > on timestamps yourself: it handles the tie, where the tombstone wins.
In select, skip rows outside the slice with the given inSlice only when filteringReason(q) is null. A filtering query reads every row of the partition, and that cost is the point of the test.
In compact, v.deadSince(now) is null for a live row. Drop a row when deadSince + gcGraceSeconds <= now.

drill.title: Claim a key once, and follow a delete to the end
drill.prompt: From memory, write the CQL table for AP4 (an idempotency key and the payment it created), the statement that claims a key exactly once and expires after 24 hours, and what the reply looks like when the key is taken. Then list, in order, what happens to a row from DELETE until it's gone from disk.

answer.html: CREATE TABLE payments.idempotency_keys ( idem_key text PRIMARY KEY, payment_id text ); INSERT INTO payments.idempotency_keys (idem_key, payment_id) VALUES ('idem-7f3a', 'pay-81723') IF NOT EXISTS USING TTL 86400; -- [applied] | idem_key | payment_id when the key is taken: -- False | idem-7f3a | pay-81723 the reply carries the winner -- a DELETE, from start to end: -- 1. a tombstone with the delete's timestamp goes to the commit log and memtable of each replica -- 2. reads see it shadow every older version of the row, and count it as a tombstone -- 3. flushes and compactions carry it along for gc_grace_seconds (864000 s, 10 days) -- 4. repair spreads it to any replica that missed it, inside those 10 days -- 5. after that, the next compaction of its files drops the tombstone and the row together

recap: A Cassandra table is a map of partitions. The partition key is hashed to a token that picks the replicas; inside a partition, rows are sorted by the clustering columns, so a range read is one slice. Wide-column is not columnar. A partition never splits: rows = write rate × bucket length, kept under 100,000 rows and 100 MB.

Writes never edit in place: commit log, memtable, then an immutable SSTable. INSERT and UPDATE are both upserts, every cell carries a write timestamp (client-side in the Java driver), and reads merge pieces from several SSTables, newest timestamp wins.
Compaction merges SSTables and drops superseded cells. STCS is the 5.0.9 cassandra.yaml default; UCS, new in 5.0, is recommended for most workloads and is the default in cassandra_latest.yaml.
A delete or an expired TTL is a tombstone, kept for gc_grace_seconds (10 days) so repair can spread it. Repair more often than that, or deleted rows come back as zombies.

Insert-then-delete on one partition causes tombstone storms: a warning past 1,000 tombstones in a read, failure past 100,000. Use Kafka for queues, time buckets with TTLs, and slices that start after the dead rows.

Off the key: ALLOW FILTERING scans every partition (fine only inside one partition), an SAI index still asks every node, and IF NOT EXISTS is a Paxos-backed lightweight transaction for the few writes that must not race.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Deletes in Cassandra are free, they return in a millisecond. Let's keep pending payouts in a table and delete each one when it's paid." Explain what a delete really writes, why it has to, and what this design does to the worker's reads after a few days.
explain.answer: A delete in Cassandra doesn't remove anything. It writes a tombstone, a marker with a timestamp, through the normal write path, which is why it's fast. It has to be a write because the data lives on three replicas: if the replicas that saw the delete just forgot the row, repair would find it on a replica that was down and copy it back. The tombstone is newer than the row, so it wins the merge and repair spreads it instead. Cassandra keeps tombstones for gc_grace_seconds, 10 days by default, before compaction may drop them. In a queue partition, every paid payout leaves a tombstone at the front, and the worker's "next 10" read starts at the front, so it steps over all of them. At 30,000 payouts a day, the read meets 30,000 tombstones after one day, logs warnings past 1,000, and fails outright past 100,000, after about four days. I'd keep the queue in Kafka, or bucket the table by hour with a TTL and have the worker read from its last position, so no read ever starts in the dead rows.

deeper.html:
Cassandra 5.0 also ships newer storage formats that its default cassandra.yaml leaves off. The cassandra_latest.yaml in the same 5.0.9 image turns them on: trie-based memtables (TrieMemtable), the BTI SSTable format (sstable: selected_format: bti, a trie-indexed format that replaces the old partition index and summary files) and UCS as the default compaction. The default file sets storage_compatibility_mode: CASSANDRA_4, so a cluster upgraded from 4.x keeps writing files 4.x could read; that's why the Try-it's files are named nb-...-big-.... A new cluster can start from cassandra_latest.yaml instead.

Two tools from the Try-its are worth keeping. sstablepartitions, new in 5.0, lists the largest partitions in an SSTable, which is how you find the account that broke the 100 MB guideline before it hurts. sstablemetadata prints, among other things, an estimate of droppable tombstones per file.

Materialized views were Cassandra's attempt to maintain lesson 2's "one table per query" for you: you declare a view with a different primary key and the server writes it. The Cassandra docs still mark them experimental, and most teams write the extra tables from the application, often in a logged batch. A logged batch guarantees that if any statement in it is applied, all of them eventually are, which is what you want when one payment goes to three tables. It isn't isolated: a reader can see one table updated before the other.

ScyllaDB speaks CQL and runs the same data model on a C++ engine, so this lesson's tables and queries work there unchanged. Since its 2025.1 release it's source-available rather than open source.
